paragraphs: My companions told me that if I visited my beloved’s grave, my sorrows would be eased a little.—Ebn Zaiat.

Misery has many shapes. The suffering of this earth takes many forms. It stretches across the wide horizon like a rainbow, its colors as varied as those of that arch—as distinct, yet as closely blended. Across the wide horizon like a rainbow! How have I taken something beautiful as an image of ugliness, a promise of peace as a comparison for sorrow? Yet just as, in moral philosophy, evil follows from good, so in life sorrow is born from joy. Either the memory of past happiness is today’s anguish, or our present agonies spring from ecstasies that might have been.

My baptismal name is Egaeus. My family name I will not mention. Yet no towers in this land are more ancient and honored than the gloomy gray halls I inherited. Our family has been called a race of visionaries, and there is more than enough striking evidence to support that belief. It is in the character of the mansion, the painted walls of the main hall, the bedroom tapestries, and the carving on some of the armory’s buttresses. But it is especially in the gallery of old paintings, the design of the library, and finally the very peculiar nature of the books it contains.

My earliest memories are bound to that room and its books, of which I will say no more. My mother died here. I was born here. But it is pointless to say I had not lived before, that the soul has no earlier existence. Do you deny it? Let us not argue. I am convinced myself and do not seek to convince others. Yet I have a memory of airy forms, of spiritual eyes filled with meaning, of sounds both musical and sad. It is a memory I cannot shut out, like a shadow: vague, changeable, shapeless, unsteady. Like a shadow, too, I cannot be rid of it while the sunlight of my reason remains.

In that room I was born. I woke from the long night of what seemed to be nonexistence, though it was not, straight into fairyland: into a palace of imagination, into the wild realms of solitary, monkish thought and learning. It is no wonder that I looked around me with startled, eager eyes, spent my boyhood lingering over books, and wasted my youth in daydreams. But as the years passed and the height of adulthood found me still in my ancestors’ mansion, something strange happened. How astonishingly the springs of my life grew stagnant! How completely the nature of my most ordinary thoughts was reversed! The realities of the world seemed to me like visions, and nothing more. Meanwhile, the wild ideas of dreams became not merely the material of my daily existence, but entirely and exclusively that existence itself.

Berenice and I were cousins, and grew up together in my father’s halls. Yet how differently we grew! I was sickly and buried in gloom; she was agile, graceful, and overflowing with energy. She wandered on the hillside; I studied in seclusion. I lived within my own heart, devoted body and soul to the most intense and painful reflection. She roamed carelessly through life, without a thought for the shadows in her path or the silent flight of the raven-winged hours. Berenice! I call her name—Berenice!—and the sound startles a thousand turbulent recollections from the gray ruins of memory. Ah, how vividly I see her now, as she was in her early days of lightheartedness and joy! Oh, splendid, dreamlike beauty! Oh, air spirit among the shrubberies of Arnheim! Oh, water nymph among its fountains! And then—then everything is mystery and terror, and a story that should not be told. Disease, a fatal disease, struck her body like a burning desert wind. Even as I watched, the spirit of change swept over her, entering her mind, her habits, and her character. In the most subtle and terrible way, it disturbed even her very identity. Alas, the destroyer came and went! And the victim—where is she? I did not know her, or no longer knew her as Berenice.

That first, fatal illness, which changed my cousin so horribly in mind and body, brought many other disorders in its wake. Among the most distressing and persistent was a kind of epilepsy that often ended in a trance closely resembling death. Her recovery from it was usually startlingly sudden. Meanwhile my own disease—for I have been told I must call it nothing else—my own disease rapidly worsened. At last it took the form of a single-minded obsession of a new and extraordinary kind. Growing stronger by the hour, by the moment, it finally gained the most incomprehensible power over me. This obsession, if I must call it that, consisted of a morbid sensitivity in the mental faculties that metaphysical science calls the powers of attention. You probably do not understand me. Indeed, I fear it is impossible to give an ordinary reader an adequate idea of the feverish intensity with which my powers of reflection, to avoid technical language, busied and buried themselves in contemplating even the most ordinary things in the universe.

I could reflect for long, tireless hours, my attention fixed on some trivial decoration in a book’s margin or its printed lettering. I could spend most of a summer’s day absorbed in an odd shadow falling slantwise across a tapestry or the floor. I could lose myself for a whole night watching a lamp’s steady flame or the embers of a fire; dream away entire days over the scent of a flower; repeat an ordinary word monotonously until repetition drained its sound of all meaning. I could lose every sense of movement or physical existence by stubbornly remaining absolutely still for a long time. These were a few of the most common and least harmful oddities caused by my mental condition. It was not entirely without parallel, but it certainly defied anything resembling analysis or explanation.

But do not misunderstand me. This excessive, intense, unhealthy attention to inherently trivial things must not be confused with the tendency to ponder that everyone shares, especially people with vivid imaginations. It was not even, as one might first suppose, an extreme or exaggerated version of that tendency. It was fundamentally and essentially different. An ordinary dreamer or enthusiast becomes interested in something that is usually not trivial. Without noticing, they gradually lose sight of it in a wilderness of conclusions and suggestions growing out of it. When the daydream ends, often after much pleasant indulgence, they find that its original trigger has vanished entirely from their thoughts and been forgotten. With me, the original object was always trivial, though my disordered vision distorted it and gave it an unreal importance. I drew few conclusions, if any, and those few kept stubbornly circling back to the original object. These reflections were never pleasant. At the end of a daydream, far from having faded out of sight, the object had taken on the supernaturally exaggerated fascination that dominated my disease. In short, as I have said, the mental powers most active in me were those of attention; in an ordinary daydreamer, they are those of speculation.

The books I read at that time, even if they did not actually worsen my disorder, shared many of its qualities in their imaginative, disconnected nature. Among others, I clearly remember the noble Italian Coelius Secundus Curio’s treatise “On the Vastness of the Blessed Kingdom of God”; St. Austin’s great work, the “City of God”; and Tertullian’s “On the Flesh of Christ.” In the last, this paradoxical sentence consumed all my time through many weeks of laborious, fruitless investigation: “The Son of God died; it is believable because it is absurd. And, after being buried, he rose again; it is certain because it is impossible.”

You can see, then, that only trivial things disturbed the balance of my reason. It resembled the sea cliff described by Ptolemy Hephestion, which firmly resisted human violence and the fiercer fury of water and wind, but trembled only at the touch of the flower called Asphodel. A careless thinker might assume without question that the changes illness made in Berenice’s mind would give me many subjects for the intense, abnormal contemplation I have taken such trouble to explain. Yet that was not the case at all. During the clear intervals in my illness, her misfortune did cause me pain. I took the complete ruin of her beautiful, gentle life deeply to heart, and often thought bitterly about the astonishing means by which such a strange transformation had happened so suddenly. But those reflections did not share the peculiar character of my disease. They were thoughts anyone might have had in similar circumstances. True to its nature, my disorder delighted in the less important but more startling changes to Berenice’s body: the strange, appalling distortion of her personal identity.

Even in the brightest days of her matchless beauty, I had certainly never loved her. In my strangely abnormal existence, my feelings had never belonged to the heart. My passions had always belonged to the mind. In the gray early morning, among the lattice-like shadows of the forest at noon, and in my library’s silence at night, she had passed before my eyes. I had seen her not as the living, breathing Berenice, but as a Berenice from a dream; not as a flesh-and-blood person, but as an abstract idea of one. She was not someone to admire, but someone to analyze; not someone to love, but a subject for the most obscure, though aimless, speculation. And now—now I shuddered in her presence and turned pale when she approached. Yet, bitterly mourning her ruined and desolate condition, I remembered that she had loved me for a long time. In an evil moment, I spoke to her of marriage.

At last our wedding drew near. One winter afternoon, on one of those unseasonably warm, calm, misty days that nurture the beautiful Halcyon bird, I sat in the library’s inner room. I thought I was alone. But when I raised my eyes, I saw Berenice standing before me.

Was it my own feverish imagination, the hazy air, the room’s uncertain twilight, or the gray fabric falling around her figure that made her outline so wavering and indistinct? I could not tell. She said nothing, and I could not have uttered a syllable for anything in the world. An icy chill ran through my body. Unbearable anxiety oppressed me. A consuming curiosity filled my soul. Sinking back in my chair, I remained breathless and motionless for some time, my eyes fixed on her. Alas, she was terribly wasted. Not a trace of her former self remained in any line of her figure. At last my burning gaze fell on her face.

Her forehead was high, very pale, and strangely calm. Her once jet-black hair fell partly across it, shadowing her hollow temples with countless curls, now a vivid yellow. Their fantastic appearance clashed harshly with the sadness that ruled her face. Her eyes were lifeless, dull, and seemingly without pupils. I shrank involuntarily from their glassy stare to look at her thin, shrunken lips. They parted. In a smile with a peculiar meaning, the teeth of the changed Berenice slowly revealed themselves. God, if only I had never seen them—or had died after seeing them!

A door closing disturbed me. Looking up, I found that my cousin had left the room. But the white, ghastly apparition of her teeth had not left the disordered chamber of my brain, and I could not drive it out. There was not a speck on their surface, not a shade on their enamel, not an indentation in their edges that the time of her smile had failed to brand into my memory. I saw them now even more distinctly than I had seen them then. The teeth! The teeth! They were here, there, everywhere, visibly and tangibly before me: long, narrow, intensely white, with the pale lips twisting around them just as they had when they were first terribly revealed. Then the full fury of my obsession came upon me, and I struggled in vain against its strange, irresistible power. Among all the countless things in the outside world, I could think of nothing but the teeth. I longed for them with a frenzied desire. Every other concern and interest was swallowed up in contemplating them alone. They—they alone—stood before my mind’s eye, and they alone became the essence of my mental life. I held them in every light. I turned them to every angle. I examined their characteristics. I dwelt on their peculiarities. I considered their shape and structure. I reflected on the change in their nature. I shuddered as I imagined them capable of sensation and awareness, capable even of expressing thoughts and feelings without the lips’ help. It has aptly been said of Mademoiselle Salle, “Every one of her steps was a feeling.” Of Berenice I believed, more seriously, that every one of her teeth was an idea. Ideas! Ah, that was the insane thought that destroyed me! Ideas! Ah, that was why I wanted them so madly! I felt that only possessing them could ever give me peace by restoring my reason.

Evening closed around me in that state. Darkness came, lingered, and went. Day dawned again. The mists of a second night were gathering around me, and still I sat motionless in that lonely room, still buried in thought. Still the phantom teeth held their terrible power, floating with the most vivid, hideous clarity among the room’s changing lights and shadows. At last a cry, as if of horror and dismay, broke into my dreams. After a pause came troubled voices mixed with many low moans of sorrow or pain. I rose, threw open one of the library doors, and saw a young maid standing in the outer room, in tears. She told me that Berenice was—no more! Epilepsy had seized her early that morning. Now, as night fell, the grave was ready for its occupant, and all the preparations for burial were complete.

I found myself sitting in the library, alone again. I seemed to have just awakened from a confused, agitating dream. I knew it was midnight, and I knew very well that Berenice had been buried since sunset. But I had no certain, at least no definite, understanding of the dreary time between. Yet its memory was full of horror: horror made more horrible by vagueness, terror made more terrible by uncertainty. It was a fearful page in the record of my life, covered with dim, hideous, incomprehensible memories. I tried to decipher them, but in vain. Every now and then, like the ghost of a vanished sound, a woman’s shrill, piercing scream seemed to ring in my ears. I had done something—what was it? I asked myself aloud. The room’s whispering echoes answered, “What was it?”

A lamp burned on the table beside me, with a little box nearby. There was nothing remarkable about it. I had seen it often before, since it belonged to the family doctor. But how had it come to be on my table, and why did I shudder when I looked at it? I could not explain these things at all. At last my eyes dropped to an open book and an underlined sentence on its pages. They were the poet Ebn Zaiat’s strange but simple words: “My companions told me that if I visited my beloved’s grave, my sorrows would be eased a little.” Why, then, as I read them, did my hair stand on end and the blood freeze in my veins?

A light tap came at the library door. A servant entered on tiptoe, as pale as the occupant of a tomb. His face was wild with terror, and his voice shook, husky and very low. What did he say? I heard a few broken sentences. He spoke of a wild cry breaking the night’s silence, of the household gathering, of a search in the direction of the sound. Then his voice grew chillingly clear as he whispered of a grave broken open, of a disfigured body wrapped in a shroud, yet still breathing—its heart still beating—still alive!

He pointed to clothes, muddy and clotted with blood. I said nothing. He gently took my hand; human nails had left their marks pressed into it. He drew my attention to something against the wall. I stared at it for several minutes. It was a spade. With a shriek, I leaped to the table and seized the box. But I could not force it open. In my trembling, it slipped from my hands, fell heavily, and shattered. With a rattling sound, dental instruments rolled out, mixed with thirty-two small, white, ivory-like objects that scattered across the floor.
